newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba's Issing lashes out at stability pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba's Issing lashes out at stability pact.

text.p: The Bundesbank's chief economist has lashed out at a European budget pact agreed on Friday, saying the deal still holds the risk that governments could be given political licence to overspend.

Otmar Issing, in an interview in Tuesday's Financial Times newspaper, said the stability pact deal did not go far enough to prevent European nations from running up budget deficits and that this meant the future European central bank could be overburdened in its main duty of keeping inflation in check.

The most worrying point of the pact, hailed by political leaders around Europe as an important step towards monetary union, was its failure to provide automatic sanctions to countries which failed to keep their spending in check, the central banker said.

Issing told the British newspaper: "Unrestrained automaticity would not have been possible but one cannot be satisfied with a decision mechanism in which potential sinners pass judgement on actual sinners."

Under the terms of the pact, countries which run a budget deficit of more than three percent of gross domestic product will face sanctions and fines unless they are forced to overspend by circumstances beyond their control or their economy contracts by two percent or more in a year.
But a country whose economy contracts by just 0.75 percent or more in a year can plead for political clemency to exempt it from the penalties.

Germany had originally sought fully automatic sanctions for countries failing to keep their budgets under control, but was forced in marathon negotiations with nearly all of Europe united against it to give politicians some jurisdiction.
In the Bundesbank's view, this weakens the pact as factors other than pure economics will likely hold sway.
"The hard task ahead will be to implement the pact in such a way that it will be difficult to make purely political decisions. The debate is not over yet," Issing said.

The Bundesbank economist went on to link the risk of budget deficits with the future European Central Bank (ECB), which will bear responsibility for European price stability after monetary union starts.
"The danger that too much pressure would be put on the monetary policy of the European central bank has not been eliminated," he said.
Private economists, who have been waiting for the Bundesbank to pass judgement on the stability pact, said they were surprised at the strength of Issing's remarks.
"This is a surprisingly harsh tone for such a senior Bundesbank official," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merill Lynch in Frankfurt.
The central banker's view of the pact carried additional punch because German politicians had hailed the stability pact deal as a resounding accomplishment.
"It is a great success, and a great personal success for (finance minister) Theo Waigel," German chancellor Helmut Kohl told a press conference in Dublin on Friday.
Issing's remarks about the inflation-fighting abilities of the ECB strike directly at a debate between Germany and France about how exactly European monetary policy will be formulated.
Whereas the Bundesbank is adamant that the central bank must be fully independent, France has called for a political body similar to the Group of Seven to counterbalance monetary policy makers.
Such a body, analysts believe, could hinder the European Central Bank's freedom to conduct policy -- especially in the field of exchange rates.

The Bundesbank, which under the Bundesbank law of 1958 is legally bound to defend the value of the mark, is opposed to French methods of foreign exchange management where politicians see the value of the franc as a tool to pursue economic goals.
